gist: Andy Burnham faced criticism following an influencer's video recorded outside Downing Street.
Critics accused the Prime Minister of prioritising social media outreach over traditional journalistic scrutiny.
Downing Street maintains it will not alter its social media communication strategy.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Max Balegde, a social media personality, deleted a video filmed outside Downing Street after attending an event there. The clip generated criticism from political rivals, including Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, who accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of turning No 10 into a joke. Downing Street stated the video was unacceptable.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Critics and political journalists argue that relying on influencers allows politicians to bypass tough scrutiny. Unlike journalists, content creators may accept restrictions, such as submitting questions beforehand. Media figures warned that prioritising unscrutinised access over independent questioning harms the public and weakens democratic accountability.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Despite the backlash, Downing Street has no intention of shifting its social media strategy. However, Burnham's team may vet future influencers more carefully to avoid further controversies regarding offensive material.

sections.text: Virginia Tech researchers used Sentinel-1 satellite radar data to track land movement in 20 African coastal cities. sections.text: Subsidence lowers land relative to the sea, compounding climate-driven sea level rises. Alexandria faces sea level rises 36% higher by 2050 than previously projected.
